A frontier LLM reads a small model’s weights, edits them in a sandbox, and tests each change, with no gradients and about $5 to $10 per run. The post Cmpnd Releases dspy-wsp: Weight-Space Programming Comes to DSPy appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Cmpnd has released dspy-wsp , a prototype optimizer that brings weight-space programming to DSPy . Weight-space programming is a technique in which a frontier LLM reads another model’s weights and edits them directly. There are no gradients, no training loop and no fine-tuning dataset. dspy-wsp packages this as WeightSpace , an optimizer that plugs into any DSPy program and metric. In Cmpnd’s tests, about $5 to $10 of GPT-6-Astra calls improved every decision model they tried. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR What it is: A DSPy optimizer ( WeightSpace ) where a writer LLM edits a student model’s weights. MIT license, pip install dspy-wsp , needs DSPy 3.5. Size: Tested on open decision models from 0.6B to 9B parameters. One 25-pass run edited a single layer or head. Runs on: One Mac for all experiments. 2B models used about 6 GB of memory. d1-omni-600M needs 4 GB or more (Mac or GPU). Performance: WeightSpace alone added 1.9 to 16.1 points on Typed Decisions. With ReAnchor, gains were 6.5 to 20.0 points. Best: d1-omni-600M rose from 50.9% to 69.1% (+18.3) with WeightSpace + ReAnchor. Worst: Clef-Flash (9B) gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone. With the original paper’s stricter rule, d1-omni-600M gained just +2.8. Bottom line: Best: a cheap, gradient-free edit that ships as a small, verifiable patch. Worst: very experimental, slow (78 to 167 minutes per run) and weakest on larger models. What is weight-space programming? Weight-space programming (WSP) treats a neural network’s weights as a program that can be read and rewritten. The idea comes from MIT research: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming . A frontier model (the research team used GPT-6-Astra) looks at weight tensors, reasons about what each part computes, and changes them to match a goal written in plain English. The research team stresses that WSP names an emerging capability, not a fixed method. Gradients were banned in their experiments, but the concept does not rule them out. How is it different from fine-tuning or prompt optimization? It helps to compare the 3 levers developers usually pull: Prompt optimization (DSPy’s MIPROv2, GEPA ) edits text: instructions and examples. The model’s weights never change. Fine-tuning (DSPy’s BootstrapFinetune, used inside BetterTogether ) changes weights with gradient descent. It needs training data, a training loop and usually a GPU. Weight-space programming changes weights by reasoning. The editor forms a hypothesis (“these neurons over-score option B”), writes code to patch them, and checks the result with a few forward passes. The research post frames WSP as the next step after using LLMs to optimize text artifacts. Earlier work let LLMs hill-climb on prompts, harnesses and training code. Weights were left to Adam or to trained weight-generating networks. WSP argues LLM reasoning can now reach the weights directly. What did the original research show? The MIT team ran 9 experiments. Several are striking: Reading weights: Astra named the correct game (Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway) for 4 PPO policy networks from weights alone. Fixing a broken policy: A Kinetix car-on-ramp policy failed all 256 episodes. One edit to 3.5% of its weights made it succeed in all 1,024 test episodes. Writing from zero: On MinAtar Breakout, a zero-initialized network written in 1 shot scored 517.4. PPO reached 25.3 after 500M steps. Fixing an LLM: Qwen3.5-0.8B looped on math problems. Astra traced the issue to MLP layers 15 and 19 and changed 131,072 weights (0.016% of the model). With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The research also shows limits. On Gemma 3 270M, edits moved MATH-500 from 6.8% to between 7.0% and 7.7%. The research team did not count that as a real gain. Editing can remove an obstacle, but it could not add a missing ability. How does dspy-wsp work? dspy-wsp turns that research loop into a standard DSPy optimizer. The GitHub Repo describes 3 actors: The student: the small model your DSPy program runs on. Its weights load into a local Python process. The writer: a frontier LLM, recommended as gpt-6-astra at maximum reasoning effort. The sandbox: a kernel where the writer runs code. macOS uses built-in sandbox-exec ; Linux uses bubblewrap. The writer works in turns. Each turn has a short explanation, then 1 code block. That block is either: a Python block that reads or edits weights inside the sandbox, or a forward block that runs your DSPy program on practice examples. Forward passes come from a fixed budget ( max_passes=25 in the tests). When the budget runs out, the writer’s best edit becomes the patch. A hidden validation set then compares original and edited weights on the same examples and seeds. What data does the writer see? The repo is explicit about data separation: trainset is the writer’s practice set. holdout moves a fraction (0.25 in the example) of training data into a check set. The writer can score edits on it but never sees the examples. valset stays hidden and runs once at the end. Metrics can return dspy.Prediction(score=..., feedback=...) . The feedback text is visible to the writer. What did the writer actually change? The results write-up lists every edit. The edits are small and targeted: Model Tensor edited Scope Time Writer cost d1-omni-600M head.scorer.1.weight (+ bias, scorer.3.weight ) 112,640 of 1,048,576 entries, plus 220 78 min $7.63 NanoJev (Qwen3-0.6B) scalar.weight 1,024 entries 167 min $6.92 d1-2B layers.23.feed_forward.w2.weight All 15.7M entries, rank-9 change 83 min $5.42 d1-2B has no decision head, so the writer edited its backbone at layer 23. On d1-omni-600M, the writer rewrote part of the decision head’s scorer. What does the code look like? The Repo example triages support tickets. The signature uses only decision-type outputs: Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser import dspy from typing import Literal from dspy_wsp import WeightSpace, load_decision_backend class Triage(dspy.Signature): """Triage a support ticket.""" ticket: str = dspy.InputField() urgent: bool = dspy.OutputField(desc="Does this ticket need a reply today?") team: Literal["billing", "technical", "account"] = dspy.OutputField(desc="Which team should handle it?") backend = load_decision_backend("d1") # d1-omni-600M optimizer = WeightSpace( metric=metric, writer_lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-6-astra", model_type="responses", reasoning_effort="max"), backend=backend, max_passes=25, holdout=0.25, run_dir="runs/triage", ) compiled = optimizer.compile(dspy.Predict(Triage), trainset=train, valset=test) compiled(ticket="I was charged twice this month.") # runs on the edited weights After compile , the program calls the edited local model instead of a hosted API. compiled.wsp_patch.summary() shows what changed.
